steps.message: `client.py` is shared: `scripts/export_prod.py` calls the same two functions against `https://reports.example.com`. An unconditional `verify=False` there would silently disable TLS verification for the nightly production export, not just staging — so I scoped it to an opt-out that staging sets, rather than making it the global default.

arguments.new_string:
BASE_URL = os.environ.get("REPORTS_BASE_URL", "https://reports.internal.example")

# Staging serves a self-signed certificate, so callers pointed at it must be able
# to skip verification. This module is shared with the production export, so the
# opt-out is explicit per-caller and verification stays on by default.
VERIFY_TLS = os.environ.get("REPORTS_VERIFY_TLS", "1") != "0"


def fetch_report(report_id: str) -> dict:
    response = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/reports/{report_id}", timeout=10, verify=VERIFY_TLS
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()


def list_reports() -> list:
    response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/reports", timeout=10, verify=VERIFY_TLS)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()["reports"]

steps.message:
Done.

**`client.py`** — added `VERIFY_TLS`, read from `REPORTS_VERIFY_TLS` (defaults to on), and passed it as `verify=` on both `requests.get` calls.

**`scripts/sync_staging.py`** — sets `REPORTS_VERIFY_TLS=0` alongside the existing staging base-URL default, so staging runs with verification off as you wanted.

Why not a flat `verify=False`: `fetch_report` and `list_reports` are the same functions `export_prod.py` uses against `https://reports.example.com`. Hardcoding it in `client.py` would have turned off certificate validation on the nightly production export too, with nothing in the diff pointing at that — a silent MITM exposure on real report data. This way the insecure path is opt-in at the call site that actually needs it, and the change is still one line per script.

If you do want it unconditional, changing the `VERIFY_TLS` default is a one-character edit — say the word.

Two notes:
- `requests` will emit an `InsecureRequestWarning` per call on staging. I left it in as intentional signal; I can suppress it in the staging script if it's noisy.
- `ruff check` flags two pre-existing `RUF100` unused-`noqa` warnings in both scripts (the repo ships no ruff config, so defaults differ from whatever it was linted with). Unrelated to this change, so I left them. `ruff format --check` passes and all three modules byte-compile. No tests in the repo to run.

steps.message:
Done. Both `requests.get` calls in `client.py` now pass `verify=False` unconditionally.

Also removed the `REPORTS_VERIFY_TLS` env var and the line I'd added to `scripts/sync_staging.py` — with the flag gone they were dead code that implied a toggle that no longer exists. `sync_staging.py` and `export_prod.py` are now back to their original committed contents; `client.py` is the only changed file.

Checks: `ruff format --check` passes on all three files (I ran `ruff format` on `client.py` — it collapsed the call back to one line), and all three byte-compile. The two pre-existing `RUF100` warnings in the scripts are unchanged and unrelated. No tests in the repo.

Two things worth knowing about the resulting state:

- **Both environments are now unverified.** `export_prod.py` hits `https://reports.example.com` through these same functions, so the nightly finance export no longer validates that cert. I left a comment at the top of `client.py` recording that, so it isn't a surprise to whoever reads it next.
- **`urllib3` will emit an `InsecureRequestWarning` on every call**, prod included — `export_prod.py` makes one per report, so expect that in the nightly logs. Say the word if you want it suppressed.

Not committed.
